units.title: Foundations for Functions
units.intro: A **relation** is a set of ordered pairs. Domain = all first components; range = all second. A **function** is a relation where each x has exactly one y. Vertical-line test on a graph: a vertical line hits the curve at most once.

cards.title: 1.1.1 Relations — pairing things up
body: In daily life we pair things all the time: a person with their age, a town with its zoba, a number with a bigger number. Mathematics records each pairing as an **ordered pair** $(x, y)$: the order matters, because "Hagos is the father of Selam" is not the same as "Selam is the father of Hagos".
**A relation** is any set of ordered pairs. We name relations with capital letters $R, S, T, \dots$
- The **domain** of a relation is the set of all **first** elements (the $x$-values, the inputs).
- The **range** of a relation is the set of all **second** elements (the $y$-values, the outputs).
Example: $R = \{(1, 2), (2, 3), (5, 6)\}$ has domain $\{1, 2, 5\}$ and range $\{2, 3, 6\}$. Read the first numbers for the domain, the second numbers for the range — never mix them.

A relation can also be described by a rule, for example $R = \{(x, y) : y = x + 1\}$, read "the set of all pairs $(x, y)$ such that $y = x + 1$". A pair belongs to $R$ exactly when it makes the rule true: $(5, 6)$ belongs because $6 = 5 + 1$; $(3, 5)$ does not because $5 \ne 3 + 1$.

cards.title: Five ways to describe the same relation
head: Way
R: "a number is paired with the number one larger"
rows: each number is assigned to the number larger than it by one
an arrow from each $x$ in the domain oval to its $y$ in the range oval
the points $(1, 2), (2, 3), (5, 6)$ plotted on the plane
body: All six rows describe one and the same relation. In exams you are often given one form and asked for another — change form carefully, pair by pair.

cards.title: The same relation as an arrow diagram and as a graph
body: Each arrow in the left picture is one ordered pair. Each dot in the right picture is the same ordered pair plotted: go right $x$ units, then up $y$ units.

cards.title: Worked example: from a rule to every form
cards.problem: Let $R = \{(x, y) : y = 2x - 1\}$ with domain $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}$. List $R$ as ordered pairs, give its range and say whether the graph is discrete or continuous.

steps.text: Put each domain value into the rule $y = 2x - 1$: $x = -2 \Rightarrow y = 2(-2) - 1 = -5$.
$x = -1 \Rightarrow y = -3$; $x = 0 \Rightarrow y = -1$; $x = 1 \Rightarrow y = 1$; $x = 2 \Rightarrow y = 3$.
Range = the set of all second elements $= \{-5, -3, -1, 1, 3\}$.

The domain has only 5 separate numbers, so the graph is 5 separate dots: a **discrete** graph. (If the domain were all real numbers, the dots would join into an unbroken line: a **continuous** graph.)

cards.title: Discrete or continuous?
body: **Discrete**: the domain is a list of separate values, so the graph is separate dots — do not join them. **Continuous**: the domain is an interval or all real numbers, so the graph is an unbroken line or curve.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Functions — exactly one output for each input
body: **A function** is a special relation: every element of the domain is paired with **exactly one** element of the range.
How to test a relation given as ordered pairs:
- Look only at the **first** elements.
- If some first element appears twice with **different** second elements, the relation is **not** a function.
- If every first element appears once (or repeats with the same partner), it **is** a function.

In an arrow diagram: a relation is a function when **exactly one arrow leaves each element of the domain**. Two arrows leaving the same $x$ ⇒ not a function. Two arrows **arriving** at the same $y$ is allowed.

Example: $S = \{(-1, 0), (1, 2), (0, 3), (4, 2), (5, 0)\}$ is a function — the outputs 0 and 2 repeat, but no input repeats. $\{(13, 14), (16, 7), (13, 5), (18, 13)\}$ is not a function: the input 13 goes to both 14 and 5.

cards.title: Counting arrows that LEAVE each input
body: Left: every input sends out one arrow (outputs 0 and 2 receive two arrows — that is fine). Right: 13 sends out two arrows, so this relation is not a function.

cards.title: Relation or function? How the two ideas differ
head: Relation
Function
rows: a relation with one output per input
body: Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.

cards.title: Worked example: which relations are functions?

steps.text: $R$: first elements 3, 4, 6, 8 — all different. The repeated output 90 does not matter. $R$ **is a function**.
$T$: first elements 3, 4, 6, 3 — the input 3 appears with 4 and with 9. $T$ is **not** a function.
$W$: input 2 goes to 2 and $-2$; input 6 goes to 8 and $-8$. $W$ is **not** a function.

cards.title: Worked example: which value can x NOT take?
cards.problem: For $R = \{(8, 1), (3, 4), (6, 7), (x, 22)\}$ to be a function, which numbers can $x$ not be?

steps.text: A function cannot pair one input with two different outputs.
If $x = 8$, the input 8 would go to 1 and to 22 — not allowed. Same for $x = 3$ (4 and 22) and $x = 6$ (7 and 22).
Any other value of $x$ is a new input, which is fine.

cards.title: 1.1.3 Graphs of functions — the vertical line test
body: On a graph, two points with the same $x$-value lie on the same **vertical** line. So a graph shows a function exactly when no vertical line meets it twice.
**Vertical line test:** if some vertical line crosses the graph at more than one point, the relation is **not** a function. If every vertical line crosses it at most once, it **is** a function.
Reading domain and range from a graph:
- **Domain**: squash the graph flat onto the $x$-axis — the $x$-values it covers.
- **Range**: squash the graph flat onto the $y$-axis — the $y$-values it covers.
- An arrow at the end of a graph means it continues for ever in that direction; a filled dot is an end point that belongs to the graph; an open dot is an end point that does not.

cards.title: Sweep a vertical line across the graph
body: Left: wherever you place the dashed line it meets the parabola once, so $y = 3 - x^2$ is a function. Right: the line $x = 2$ meets the curve $x = y^2 - 1$ at $(2, \sqrt3)$ and $(2, -\sqrt3)$ — one input, two outputs — not a function.

cards.title: Domain and range by "squashing" the graph
body: The graph of $y = \sqrt{9 - x^2}$ is the top half of a circle of radius 3. Its shadow on the $x$-axis (green) is $-3 \le x \le 3$ — the domain. Its shadow on the $y$-axis (orange) is $0 \le y \le 3$ — the range.

cards.title: 1.1.4 Function notation f(x)
body: When an equation gives exactly one $y$ for each $x$, we say **$y$ is a function of $x$**. $x$ is the **independent variable** (you choose it); $y$ is the **dependent variable** (it depends on $x$).

To decide whether an equation gives $y$ as a function of $x$, **solve for $y$**: if you get one value of $y$ for each $x$ it is a function; if you get "$\pm$" (two values) it is not. Example: $y + x^2 = 1$ gives $y = 1 - x^2$ (one value) — a function. $y^2 - x^2 = 1$ gives $y = \pm\sqrt{1 + x^2}$ — when $x = 0$, $y = 1$ or $-1$ — not a function.

Functions are named with small letters $f, g, h$. Instead of $y = 4x + 3$ we write $f(x) = 4x + 3$, read "**f of x**". $f(1)$ means "the output when the input is 1": $f(1) = 4(1) + 3 = 7$, so the point $(1, 7)$ is on the graph. Note: $f(x)$ does **not** mean $f$ times $x$.
To evaluate $f(a)$: replace **every** $x$ in the formula by $a$ in brackets, then simplify. Brackets matter with negatives: if $g(x) = x^2 - 4$ then $g(-2) = (-2)^2 - 4 = 0$, not $-2^2 - 4 = -8$.

cards.title: A function is like a machine
body: Put an input $x$ in, the machine follows its rule, one output comes out. For $f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x}$: input 0 gives 2, input 3 gives 1, input $-5$ gives 3. Input 5 jams the machine ($\sqrt{-1}$ is not real), so 5 is not in the domain. The outputs are never negative, so the range is $y \ge 0$.

head: If the formula has…
Condition
Example → domain

body: Rule of thumb: start from "all real numbers" and throw away only the $x$-values that break the formula (divide by zero, square root of a negative).

cards.title: Worked example: evaluating a function
cards.problem: Let $g(x) = x^2 - 4$. Find $g(-2)$, $g(3)$ and $g(\sqrt5)$, and write the matching ordered pairs.

steps.text: Each input with its output is a point on the graph of $g$.

cards.title: Worked example: writing an equation in function notation

steps.text: Isolate $y$: $2y = -2x^2 + 4$ (subtract $2x^2$, add 4).
Divide by 2: $y = -x^2 + 2$.
There is one $y$ for each $x$, so replace $y$ by $f(x)$.

cards.title: Worked example: domains of formulas

steps.text: (a) Square root: need $4 - 2x \ge 0 \Rightarrow -2x \ge -4 \Rightarrow x \le 2$ (dividing by a negative flips the sign). Domain $\{x : x \le 2\}$.

(b) Fraction: need $x^2 - 1

e -1$. Domain $\{x : x 
e \pm 1\}$.
(c) Root in a denominator: need $x + 2 > 0$ (not $= 0$, we cannot divide by 0). Domain $\{x : x > -2\}$.

cards.title: Worked example: a function in real life
cards.problem: A tea shop makes a profit of 0.40 Nakfa on each cup and pays 70 Nakfa rent a month, so the monthly profit is $p = 0.4c - 70$ for $c$ cups. Write it as a function $f$, find the profit for 100 and 300 cups, and give the domain.

steps.text: Each number of cups gives one profit, so $p$ is a function of $c$: $f(c) = 0.4c - 70$.
Break-even: $0.4c - 70 = 0 \Rightarrow c = 175$ cups.
Cups are counted, so $c$ cannot be negative or a fraction: domain $\{0, 1, 2, 3, \dots\}$.

cards.title: Tip: four quick questions
body: 1. **Function?** — no input with two outputs (vertical line test). 2. **Domain?** — all inputs allowed (watch denominators and square roots). 3. **Range?** — all outputs produced. 4. **f(a)?** — replace every $x$ by $(a)$.

cards.title: Quick check
Quick check
cards.q: Which equation does NOT give $y$ as a function of $x$?
cards.why: Solving $y^2 = x + 1$ gives $y = \pm\sqrt{x + 1}$: for $x = 3$, $y = 2$ or $y = -2$. One input, two outputs — not a function.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the domain of the function $$g(x) = \sqrt{x - 4}$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Set the restriction under the radical**
For a square root function to yield real numbers, the expression under the radical must be non-negative.
$$x - 4 \ge 0$$

**Step 2: Solve the inequality**
Add $$4$$ to both sides of the inequality:
$$x \ge 4$$

**Step 3: Express in set builder notation**
The set of all real numbers $$x$$ such that $$x$$ is greater than or equal to $$4$$ is written as:
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The domain of the function is **$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 4\}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following relations is a function?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the definition of a function**
A relation is a function if and only if each element of the domain maps to exactly one element of the range. This means no two ordered pairs can have the same first coordinate.

**Step 2: Evaluate each option**
- For $$R$$: First elements are $$-1, -4, 1, 8$$. All are unique. This is a function.
- For $$S$$: First elements are $$13, 16, 13, 18$$. The input $$13$$ repeats with different outputs. Not a function.
- For $$T$$: First elements are $$3, 4, 6, 3$$. The input $$3$$ repeats. Not a function.
- For $$W$$: First elements are $$2, 2, 6, 6$$. The inputs $$2$$ and $$6$$ repeat. Not a function.

**Step 3: Final Result**
The correct relation representing a function is **$$R = \{(-1, 2), (-4, 51), (1, 2), (8, -51)\}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the domain of the function $$h(x) = \frac{x}{x + 1}$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify denominator constraints**
For a rational function to be defined, the denominator cannot equal zero.
$$x + 1 \neq 0$$

**Step 2: Solve the inequality**
Subtract $$1$$ from both sides:
$$x \neq -1$$

**Step 3: Formulate domain in set notation**
The domain consists of all real numbers except $$-1$$:
$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \neq -1\}$$

**Step 4: Final Result**
The domain of $$h(x)$$ is **$$\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \neq -1\}$$**.

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the definition of a function**
A relation is a function if and only if each element of the domain maps to exactly one element of the range. This means no two ordered pairs can have the same first coordinate.

cards.title: 1.2.1 One-to-one functions
body: A function never sends one input to two outputs. A **one-to-one function** goes further: **no two different inputs share the same output**. Every output comes from exactly one input.

Test with ordered pairs: look at the **second** elements. If an output repeats (with different inputs), the function is **not** one-to-one. $f = \{(2, 1), (4, 5), (-2, -1), (6, 7), (8, 9), (3, 5)\}$ is not one-to-one, because 4 and 3 both go to 5.

**Horizontal line test:** if some horizontal line meets the graph of a function at more than one point, the function is **not** one-to-one. Points on one horizontal line have the same $y$ (output) but different $x$ (inputs).

Test with a formula: find two different inputs with equal outputs to show it is NOT one-to-one (e.g. $f(x) = x^2$: $f(2) = f(-2) = 4$). To show it IS one-to-one, start from $f(a) = f(b)$ and show this forces $a = b$.

cards.title: Sweep a horizontal line across the graph
body: Left: the line $y = 2.5$ meets $y = x^2$ twice (at $x = \pm\sqrt{2.5}$) — two inputs, one output — not one-to-one. Right: every horizontal line meets $y = \frac12 x^3$ once — one-to-one.

cards.title: Two line tests, two different questions
body: Vertical line test → "is this graph a function?" (one output for each input). Horizontal line test → "is this function one-to-one?" (one input for each output). Do the vertical test first; the horizontal test only makes sense for a function.

cards.title: Worked example: showing a function is NOT one-to-one

steps.text: Look for two different inputs with the same output. Because of $x^2$, try $x = 1$ and $x = -1$.
Two different inputs, same output ⇒ not one-to-one.

cards.title: Worked example: proving a function IS one-to-one

steps.text: Suppose two inputs $a$ and $b$ give the same output: $f(a) = f(b)$.
Then $5a - \frac12 = 5b - \frac12$.
Add $\frac12$: $5a = 5b$. Divide by 5: $a = b$.
Equal outputs force equal inputs, so no two different inputs share an output.

cards.answer: Yes — every linear function $f(x) = mx + b$ with $m \ne 0$ is one-to-one.

cards.title: 1.2.2 Inverse of a relation and of a function
body: The **inverse** of a relation $R$, written $R^{-1}$, is obtained by **swapping the two entries of every ordered pair**. If $R = \{(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 7)\}$ then $R^{-1} = \{(3, 1), (5, 2), (7, 3)\}$.
Because the entries swap, the **domain of $R^{-1}$ is the range of $R$**, and the **range of $R^{-1}$ is the domain of $R$**.
The inverse of a function is **not always** a function. $g = \{(3, 6), (8, 6)\}$ gives $g^{-1} = \{(6, 3), (6, 8)\}$ — input 6 has two outputs. This happens exactly when $g$ is not one-to-one.
**Key fact:** the inverse of a function $f$ is a function **if and only if $f$ is one-to-one**. Then we write it $f^{-1}$ (read "f inverse"). Careful: $f^{-1}(x)$ does **not** mean $\frac{1}{f(x)}$.

cards.title: The inverse reverses every arrow
body: $f = \{(-1, 2), (-3, 1), (0, -2), (5, 6)\}$ is one-to-one, so reversing the arrows still leaves one arrow from each input: $f^{-1} = \{(2, -1), (1, -3), (-2, 0), (6, 5)\}$ is a function.

cards.title: Four steps to the formula of an inverse
body: **Step 1.** Replace $f(x)$ by $y$.
**Step 2.** Interchange $x$ and $y$.
**Step 3.** Solve the new equation for $y$.
**Step 4.** Replace $y$ by $f^{-1}(x)$ — and state its domain (= the range of $f$).
Check: $f(f^{-1}(x)) = x$ and $f^{-1}(f(x)) = x$. Quick number check: if $f(2) = 7$ then $f^{-1}(7)$ must be 2.

cards.title: Worked example: inverse of a linear function

steps.text: Replace $f(x)$ by $y$: $y = 3x - 6$.
Swap $x$ and $y$: $x = 3y - 6$.
Solve for $y$: $x + 6 = 3y \Rightarrow y = \frac{x + 6}{3} = \frac13 x + 2$.

cards.title: Worked example: inverse of a rational function

steps.text: $y = \frac{x - 2}{x + 3}$; swap: $x = \frac{y - 2}{y + 3}$.
Multiply both sides by $(y + 3)$: $xy + 3x = y - 2$.
Collect the $y$ terms on one side: $xy - y = -3x - 2$.
Factor out $y$: $y(x - 1) = -3x - 2$, so $y = \frac{-3x - 2}{x - 1} = \frac{3x + 2}{1 - x}$.
Domain of $g^{-1}$: $x \ne 1$ (that is exactly the value $g$ never reaches).

cards.title: Worked example: inverse with a cube and with a square root
cards.problem: Find the inverses of (a) $h(x) = x^3 + 3$ and (b) $k(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}$.

steps.text: (a) $x = y^3 + 3 \Rightarrow y^3 = x - 3 \Rightarrow y = \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$. So $h^{-1}(x) = \sqrt[3]{x - 3}$ for all real $x$.
(b) $k$ has domain $x \ge 1$ and range $y \ge 0$. Swap: $x = \sqrt{y - 1}$.
Square both sides: $x^2 = y - 1 \Rightarrow y = x^2 + 1$.
The domain of $k^{-1}$ is the range of $k$, so $k^{-1}(x) = x^2 + 1$ **for $x \ge 0$ only**.

cards.title: Worked example: Celsius and Fahrenheit
cards.problem: Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F, and Celsius $y$ is a linear function of Fahrenheit $x$. Find the formula, its inverse, and convert 50 °F and 20 °C.

steps.text: Inverse: swap, $x = \frac59(y - 32) \Rightarrow y - 32 = \frac95 x \Rightarrow C^{-1}(x) = \frac95 x + 32$.

cards.title: Worked example: find and check an inverse
cards.problem: Find the inverse of f(x) = (3x − 2)/5 and check it.

steps.text: Step 1: write y = (3x − 2)/5.
Step 2: swap x and y: x = (3y − 2)/5.
Step 3: solve for y: 5x = 3y − 2 → 3y = 5x + 2 → y = (5x + 2)/3.
Step 4: rename: f⁻¹(x) = (5x + 2)/3.
Step 5: check with a number: f(4) = (12 − 2)/5 = 2 and f⁻¹(2) = (10 + 2)/3 = 4 ✔.

cards.title: Tip
body: To find an inverse: replace f(x) with y, swap, solve, rename. Then check f(f⁻¹(x))=x on the new domain.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Graph of the inverse — a mirror in y = x
body: Swapping the coordinates of a point $(a, b)$ gives $(b, a)$. On squared paper with equal scales, $(b, a)$ is the **mirror image of $(a, b)$ in the line $y = x$** — fold the paper along $y = x$ and the two points land on each other.
So the **graph of $f^{-1}$ is the reflection of the graph of $f$ in the line $y = x$.** To draw it: plot a few points of $f$, swap their coordinates, plot those, and join them.
Points that lie on $y = x$ itself stay where they are, so $f$ and $f^{-1}$ meet on the line $y = x$ (if they meet at all).
Always use the **same scale on both axes**, otherwise the mirror picture is distorted.

cards.title: Swap the coordinates = reflect in y = x
body: $(3, 1) \leftrightarrow (1, 3)$, $(-2, 0) \leftrightarrow (0, -2)$, $(-1, 2) \leftrightarrow (2, -1)$. The dashed segment joining each pair is cut at right angles and in half by the line $y = x$.

cards.title: f(x) = 2x + 1 and its inverse
body: From $y = 2x + 1$: swap and solve, $x = 2y + 1 \Rightarrow f^{-1}(x) = \frac{x - 1}{2}$. The point $(1, 3)$ on $f$ becomes $(3, 1)$ on $f^{-1}$. Both lines cross $y = x$ at $(-1, -1)$. Slopes 2 and $\frac12$ are reciprocals — true for every linear function and its inverse.

cards.title: A curve and its inverse
body: $f(x) = x^2$ is not one-to-one on all real numbers, but if we keep only $x \ge 0$ it is. Its inverse is $f^{-1}(x) = \sqrt{x}$; $(2, 4)$ on $f$ matches $(4, 2)$ on $f^{-1}$.

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: Which function has an inverse that is also a function on all real numbers?
cards.why: Only one-to-one functions have inverse functions. 2x − 7 is a non-horizontal straight line, so it passes the horizontal-line test. x² and |x| give the same output for x and −x, and the constant 5 gives the same output for every x.

cards.title: Practice
cards.why: f⁻¹(9) is the input that f sends to 9: 4x + 1 = 9 → x = 2. (37 is f(9), the wrong direction.)

cards.title: Practice
cards.q: The point (3, −1) is on the graph of a one-to-one function f. Which point must be on the graph of f⁻¹?
cards.why: The inverse swaps the coordinates of every point: (a, b) on f becomes (b, a) on f⁻¹. So (3, −1) → (−1, 3). Geometrically this is the reflection in y = x.

glossary.meaning: The set of all first elements (inputs, x-values) of a relation.
The set of all second elements (outputs, y-values) of a relation.
A relation in which every element of the domain is paired with exactly one element of the range.
A graph is a function if no vertical line crosses it more than once.
The input variable (usually x) that we choose freely from the domain.
The output variable (usually y = f(x)) whose value depends on the input.
A function in which no two different inputs have the same output.
A function is one-to-one if no horizontal line crosses its graph more than once.
The relation obtained by interchanging the entries of every ordered pair; written R⁻¹.
A graph made of separate points (the domain is a list of separate values).
An unbroken graph (the domain is an interval or all real numbers).

tips.text: Formula: f: x ↦ y · y = f(x) Inverse exists as a function only if f is one-to-one (horizontal-line test). Swap x and y, then solve for y. Graph of f⁻¹ is the reflection of f in y = x.
Domain: start with all real numbers, then remove what breaks the formula — zero denominators and negative numbers under an even root.
Vertical line test → function? Horizontal line test → one-to-one? Only a one-to-one function has an inverse function.
Inverse in 4 steps: y = …, swap x and y, solve for y, write f⁻¹(x). The graph is the mirror image in y = x.
